nameStory: This wildflower gets its name from its leaves, which look remarkably similar to those of dogwood trees (also called cornels). The 'whitetop' part refers to the clusters of small white flowers that crown the plant in late summer, creating a frothy white cap above the foliage.
description: Cornel-leaf whitetop is a perennial wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall in the eastern woodlands. It produces clusters of small white daisy-like flowers at the top of its stems in late summer. The plant has distinctive oval leaves with prominent parallel veins that run from the base to the tip, giving it an almost dogwood-like appearance. It's a member of the aster family but looks quite different from the typical fall asters most people know.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with smooth edges and distinctive parallel veins running from base to tip, feeling smooth and papery when dry. The veining pattern looks almost exactly like dogwood leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white daisy-like flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters, each flower about half an inch across with white petals surrounding a yellow center.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 1-3 feet tall with a somewhat sparse, open appearance, often leaning slightly rather than standing perfectly upright.

idTips.label: Leaves Arrangement
idTips.description: Leaves alternate along the stem (not opposite each other) and gradually get smaller toward the top of the plant.

habitat: Look for cornel-leaf whitetop in dry to moderately moist woodlands, often on slopes or in clearings where some sunlight filters through. It prefers acidic soils and is typically found in oak-hickory or mixed hardwood forests. In New England, it's most likely to be encountered in the southern portions of the region.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as bright green shoots, showing their characteristic dogwood-like veining pattern early in the season.
seasonality.summer: White flower clusters appear in late summer, typically August, creating distinctive flat-topped displays above the foliage.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, with small fluffy seeds dispersing in the wind.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving no above-ground traces until spring regrowth begins.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that it's only been documented 3 times in the entire region, making it one of the most elusive wildflowers you could possibly encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: The dogwood-like leaves might make you think you're looking at a young dogwood tree, but remember that dogwoods have opposite leaves while this plant's leaves alternate along the stem. Also, dogwoods are woody shrubs or trees, while this is a soft-stemmed herbaceous plant.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'aster,' this plant was recently moved to a different genus (Doellingeria) based on genetic studies, though it's still in the same big aster family. You might see it listed in older books as Aster infirmus.
compareHints: Cornel-leaf whitetop differs from its close relative flat-top white aster by having those distinctive dogwood-like leaves with parallel veins, while flat-top white aster has more typical narrow, lance-shaped leaves with a single main vein. Both have similar white flat-topped flower clusters, but the leaf difference is unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Flat-top white aster differs from its cousin cornel-leaf whitetop by being much taller and having narrower leaves.
